notes.front: What are flow metrics in the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: Measures of how work items move through the Kanban system; the Guide requires collecting and analysing a minimum set of them.
notes.explanation: They reflect the system's current health and performance, and help inform decisions about how value is delivered.
notes.example: Like a patient's vital signs: a few readings that show how the system is doing now.

notes.front: What is Throughput?
notes.back: The number of work items finished per unit of time, measured as an exact count of items.
notes.explanation: Only finished items count, and each counts as one.
notes.example: Seven items finished this week: Throughput is 7 items per week.

notes.front: What does “velocity” usually mean when an agile coach uses the word, according to the Kanban Pocket Guide?
notes.back: Story points completed per sprint.
notes.explanation: Some people use “velocity” and “Throughput” interchangeably, which the Pocket Guide warns against when velocity means points. Story points are a team's estimate of an item's relative complexity or effort; a sprint is a fixed-length work period of one month or less in Scrum. So velocity is estimated effort finished per period, not a count of items.
notes.example: “Our velocity is 40” usually means 40 story points per sprint, not 40 items.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Throughput”; The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: What is “lead time” in Kanban University's Kanban Method?
notes.back: The time for a single work item to pass through the system, from when the team commits to it (its commitment point) to completion.
notes.explanation: It is a different term from a different body of knowledge; the Kanban Guide itself uses Cycle Time.
notes.example: A request is accepted on the 1st and delivered on the 15th: in that approach, a lead time of 14 days.
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 Kanban University, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is collecting and analysing flow metrics optional in Kanban, per the Guide?
notes.back: No. The application of Kanban requires collecting and analysing a minimum set of flow metrics.
notes.explanation: Without them, members cannot see the system's health or use data to inform decisions.

notes.front: How many mandatory flow metrics does the Kanban Guide name?
notes.back: Four: WIP, Throughput, Work Item Age and Cycle Time.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls them the four mandatory flow metrics to track in Kanban.

notes.front: How does the Guide define WIP as a flow metric?
notes.back: The number of work items started but not finished.
notes.explanation: It is a count of items between the started and finished points defined in the DoW.

notes.front: The flow metric that counts items started but not yet finished is {{c1::WIP}}.
notes.explanation: The other three are two elapsed times (Work Item Age and Cycle Time) and one rate (Throughput).

notes.front: The flow metric measured from an item's start to the current date is {{c1::Work Item Age}}.
notes.explanation: It only applies to items still in progress.

notes.front: The flow metric measured from an item's start to its finish is {{c1::Cycle Time}}.
notes.explanation: It only applies to finished items.

notes.front: The flow metric that counts items finished per unit of time is {{c1::Throughput}}.
notes.explanation: It is the only one of the four that is a rate.

notes.front: What does the Guide say Throughput is measured in?
notes.back: The exact count of work items.
notes.explanation: Not story points, hours or any other estimate: just how many items finished.

notes.front: May a team call Cycle Time “Flow Time”, or Throughput “Delivery Rate”?
notes.back: Yes, provided the metrics are used as the Guide describes; members may use any names they choose.
notes.explanation: The Guide itself gives these two examples of other names.

notes.front: In the four flow metrics, what do “started” and “finished” mean?
notes.back: Whatever the Kanban system members have defined them to be in their DoW.
notes.explanation: The metrics have no universal start and end; they inherit the DoW's started and finished points.

notes.front: When does the Guide say the flow metrics are meaningless?
notes.back: When they cannot inform one or more of the three Kanban practices.
notes.explanation: Metrics exist to drive action on the workflow, not to be reported for their own sake.

notes.front: Who decides how best to use the flow metrics, for example in charts or by assessing variation?
notes.back: The Kanban system members.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires the metrics but leaves how to leverage them to the members.

notes.front: Are the four flow metrics the most a Kanban team should track?
notes.back: No. They are only the minimum; members may, and often should, add context-specific measures.
notes.explanation: Extra measures are welcome if they help make data-informed decisions.

notes.front: Does Cycle Time count only the time someone was actively working on an item?
notes.back: No. It is elapsed time, so waiting and delay count too.
notes.explanation: The Pocket Guide notes that customers think in elapsed time, and that waiting is where most unpredictability lies: delay is the enemy of flow.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Cycle Time”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What happens to an item's Work Item Age when the item finishes?
notes.back: The age it has built up becomes its Cycle Time.
notes.explanation: Work Item Age applies only to items that have started but not finished.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Work Item Age”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which term does the Kanban Guide use for the time from start to finish: Cycle Time or lead time?
notes.back: Cycle Time. ProKanban recommends the Guide's term, with the started and finished points made explicit in the DoW.
notes.explanation: ProKanban notes that “lead time” varies by context; some teams measure it from idea submitted to customer receipt.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, “The Kanban Pocket Guide” page, FAQ
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A dashboard tile reads “Items finished per week: 9”. Which flow metric is it?
notes.back: Throughput.
notes.explanation: A count of finished items per unit of time is Throughput.

notes.front: A card on the board is labelled “in progress for 11 days”. Which flow metric is that?
notes.back: Work Item Age.
notes.explanation: The item is unfinished, so its time so far is its age, not its Cycle Time.

notes.front: A report says “Ticket 42 took 6 days from start to done”. Which flow metric is that?
notes.back: Cycle Time.
notes.explanation: The elapsed time from start to finish of a finished item is its Cycle Time.

notes.front: A daily team check-in starts with: “We have 7 items between started and finished right now.” Which flow metric is that?
notes.back: WIP.
notes.explanation: A count of items started but not finished at a point in time is WIP.

notes.front: A team tracks WIP, Throughput and Cycle Time, but not Work Item Age. Does it meet the Guide's minimum?
notes.back: No. All four flow metrics are mandatory.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: three of four is enough
B) No: all four are mandatory
C) Yes, if its Cycle Time is short
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide calls all four mandatory and the minimum required. C: nothing in the Guide makes a metric depend on performance.
notes.explanation: Work Item Age matters most for items still in progress, which the other three metrics do not show one by one.

notes.front: A team's board shows “Delivery Rate: 5 items a week” instead of “Throughput”. Is that allowed by the Guide?
notes.back: Yes, as long as it measures Throughput as the Guide describes.
notes.explanation: The Guide lets members use any names they choose for the metrics, and gives “Delivery Rate” as an example.

notes.front: Two teams both report Cycle Time, but one starts the clock at Analysis and the other at Build. Why can't their numbers be compared directly?
notes.back: Started and finished come from each team's own DoW, so each measures a different span of work.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties the flow metrics to the started and finished points each DoW defines.

notes.front: A team publishes flow charts every month, but they never lead to any change in how it works. What does the Guide say about such metrics?
notes.back: They are meaningless unless they inform one or more of the three Kanban practices.
notes.explanation: Metrics must feed defining, managing or improving the workflow to be worth tracking.

notes.front: A coach tells a team the Kanban Guide requires one particular chart for its metrics. Is that right?
notes.back: No. How to leverage the metrics, for example in charts or by assessing variation, is up to the Kanban system members.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires the metrics, not any specific chart.

notes.front: A team adds a fifth measure, “days blocked per item”. Does this go against the Guide?
notes.back: No. The four are the minimum; members may and often should add context-specific measures.
notes.explanation: Extra measures that help data-informed decisions are encouraged.

notes.front: A team reports its Throughput as “34 points this week”. What is wrong?
notes.back: Throughput is the exact count of work items finished, not a sum of points.
notes.explanation: Points are an estimate of effort; Throughput is simply how many items finished per unit of time.

notes.front: What is the difference between Work Item Age and Cycle Time?
notes.back: Work Item Age is for unfinished items (start to today); Cycle Time is for finished items (start to finish).
notes.explanation: Both are elapsed times measured from the started point defined in the DoW.

notes.front: What is the difference between Throughput and velocity, as the Pocket Guide explains it?
notes.back: Throughput counts finished items per unit of time; velocity usually sums story points per sprint, so they are not synonyms.
notes.explanation: When velocity is defined in story points, the Pocket Guide says the two are anything but synonymous.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Throughput”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between Cycle Time (Kanban Guide) and lead time (Kanban Method)?
notes.back: Cycle Time runs between the started and finished points in the DoW; lead time runs from a commitment point to completion.
notes.explanation: They come from different bodies of knowledge; for the Kanban Guide, use Cycle Time and define your points in the DoW.
